journal.text: Undersexton Aveline Rell has given me a sealed quarterly return to carry from Soulrest to the Court's factor in Gideon. She pays a hundred and twenty in advance, which is more than the work is worth, and she asked twice whether anyone had spoken to me on the stair.

The seal on the return is a mortuary seal and it is not fresh. Whatever is in it was closed up before I was hired. At the Bone Ladder the keeper asked me whose count I was carrying and would not say what she meant.
A man in a good coat walked the coast track behind me from the Ladder to Hollow-Reeds and turned back when I stopped to sit. He was not a carter and he was not going to Gideon.

The Court's factor in Gideon opened the return in front of me and read three lines of it and stopped. He said the Undersexton knows what is in her own quarterlies and did not need me to bring her one. I was not carrying a book. I was carrying a man in a good coat, from Soulrest to Gideon, to see who he was.

The factor's name for the man in the coat is Sedd Ravano and he takes money from the Wet Ledger to know what the Court is writing down. The factor says this is neither news nor a secret and that Rell has been trying to put a face to it for two seasons. I have written the name down because I do not trust myself to remember it in four days.

I put the return in the factor's hand in Gideon and said nothing about the man in the coat, and I was paid the rest of my hundred and twenty. Rell wrote something down when I told her the road had been quiet, and she did not believe me, and she hired me again anyway.

Rell wants eleven burial boxes counted and their weights written down. They came back from the wells at Bone Ladder and Salt-Egg Camp with nothing in them, which she says happens, and which she is nonetheless paying me to write down.

All eleven are empty and all eleven are the right weight for empty. The mortuary hands say the bodies went into the wells and did not come out as anything, not as sap, not as heat, not as the smell they expect. One of them would not go on talking about it inside. I weighed all eleven myself.

I sat on the burial stair after dark and there is a sound under the Stone Wastes. It is not surf and it is not wind in the salt-store. It is regular, and slow, and it has been going on longer than anyone in Soulrest has been paying attention to it.

The mortuary hand's name is Ojal-Weeth and outside, where the sound is, she said the boxes have been coming back empty for longer than eleven. She has been counting them herself since her mother died and it is not eleven, it is closer to ninety. I went outside with her because she would not say it in the shed.

Eleven boxes, eleven weights, all of them the weight of an empty box. Rell read the list twice and put it in a press that already had a great many lists in it. I gave her the list and she did not thank me for it.

Rell wants to know why the sapwell at the Bone Ladder has stopped giving. She is not sending a rootkeeper and she is not sending a sexton. She is sending me, because I owe the wells nothing and because whatever is wrong there will not have any hold on me.

The basin at the Ladder is full and the sap in it is the right colour and it does not do anything. Teeja-Lun has put her hand in it every morning for eleven days and the root has not tasted her. She has been keeping the wound open with a knife because she is afraid it will close. I put my own hand in the basin and nothing tasted me either.

Teeja-Lun says the well did not fail slowly. It gave one night and did not give the next, and the night it stopped was the night the carters heard the Wastes go quiet. Not loud. Quiet. I asked her twice and she gave me the same night both times.

Under the rib there is a shaft in the stone that is older than the road and it is not a burial. The sap in the basin is not standing still. It is going down, slowly, into something, and it has been going down since the night it stopped coming back. Whatever I do at this basin closes the others: a wound cut wider cannot be reported as a wound left alone, and a keeper protected cannot also be a keeper contradicted.

Teeja-Lun has known about the shaft her whole life. Every keeper on this coast knows. They do not speak about it because a well that drains is still a well, and a keeper who says otherwise is a keeper nobody kneels to. She told me this after I had already found it, which I notice.

I told Rell the well at the Ladder is not empty, it is draining, and that there is a shaft under the rib that the keepers have known about for generations. She did not write it down straight away. She sat with it.

Rell says I am becoming legible. A stranger who does nothing but errands for the Drowned Court is a stranger everyone can read, and she would rather I were harder to read than that. She wants me to take a name somewhere else — any name, she does not care which — so that when I am seen on a road there is another reason for it.

She was clear about one thing and I think she meant it. Whatever I swear to, she says, the Court will still have me, and if I swear to nothing the Court will still have me, and it will only cost me more later. She would not say what it would cost.
I have a name in the Wet Ledger now and a reason to be on the river that is not the Court's reason. Rell asked which one I had taken and then did not write it down, which I noticed.
Rell has sent for me to stand in the Court's chapter room while something is read out. She would not say what. She would only say that I should not answer anything anybody asks me until it is over.

The Ninth Recension of the Drowned Tally is a text the Court has been copying for four hundred years, and one clause of it was read out at me. When the tide fails, it says, the count will be read by one who is owed nothing — not of the marsh, not of the Court, and holding no debt to any root. Then everyone in the room looked at me.

I asked Rell afterwards whether she believed it. She said that what she believes is not the useful question, and that the useful question is whether the sextons believe it, and that they do, and that this is worth more than either of us being right.

The chapter room copy is in a hand I have seen before. It is the same hand as the fair copies Rell's own clerks make, and the ink on the ninth clause does not match the ink on the eighth. That proves the clause was copied later than the rest of the book. It does not prove it was invented.

There is an older recension in the Court's archive, the seventh, and the clause is in that one too, in an older hand, worded differently and meaning the same. So either the forgery is four hundred years old or it is not a forgery. I asked the archivist which and he said that this is the question the Court has been arguing about for four hundred years and that nobody has ever won it.

I stood there and let them read it and said nothing, and afterwards the Court has a tally-reader and I have a name I did not ask for. Rell says the name is worth more than the money and she is not wrong, and I notice that she never said whether it is true.

Hosk-Vei has agreed to open the Tally to me, all four hundred years of it, on the condition that I read it in the room and write nothing down that I cannot say out loud to him first. He wants the same thing I want, which is a number.

The Tally is a burial book. Every death the Court handled, what was paid, and what the wells gave back afterwards, in the Court's own units, four hundred years without a gap. It is the only continuous record of the tide in the province and nobody outside this room has ever added it up. I have been given the whole of it to read.

Adding it up took eleven days. The return per death is flat from the earliest volumes until the year thirty-nine of the third era's fourth century, and from that year it falls, and it has not stopped falling since. It is not a cliff. It is a curve, and the curve is thirty-six years old. I did the addition myself and I checked it twice.

The first licence to cut a sapwell for sale was granted in the year forty-seven. The curve begins in thirty-nine. Whatever the Sap-Cutters have done to this province, and they have done a great deal, the tide was already going before the first of them picked up a knife. I looked the licence date up before I let myself believe the rest of it.

In the older volumes there is a hand that is not a sexton's, entering corrections in the margins, always to the return column and always downward. Hosk-Vei says the Court calls that hand the Steward of the Count, and that it has been appearing in the margins of this book since the fourth volume, and that the fourth volume is three hundred and ten years old. Hosk-Vei will let me leave with the sum in my head or with it in his archive under both our names, and not both, because a fair copy is a thing the Court has said and a memory is a thing only I have.

The name in the fourth volume is Ixtu-Meer. Hosk-Vei says it is a title and not a person, the way Undersexton is a title, and then he said that if I found a sexton who had ever met a second one he would like to be told.

The curve is thirty-six years old and the cutting licences are twenty-eight. I can say that now and mean it, and I can say who has been writing corrections into the return column since before anyone alive was born. Hosk-Vei asked me to say it out loud to him twice before he would let me leave with it.

Neeja-Xul cuts sapwells for money and does not pretend otherwise. She has agreed to show me the yard and the books that go with it on one condition, which is that I bring her whatever number the Court has, because nobody has ever told the Cutters what they are supposed to have done.

The yard's own ledger goes back twenty-eight years to the first licence. Two hundred and forty wells cut, of which the yard has records of eighty still giving and sixty-one closed. That is a great deal of harm and it is not four hundred years of anything. She let me count the yard's own entries without standing over me.

Neeja-Xul says the thing nobody will hear: the wells the Cutters opened are the only wells on the coast that still give at all, because a fresh wound gives before it learns better. She thinks this is an argument. It is also, as far as I can tell, true, and it is the worst true thing I have been told this season.

Her grandmother's yard book is under the bench and it is older than the licence. The Cutters were cutting before the Empire gave anyone leave to, back into the forties, and the earliest entry in it complains that the wells that year gave less than the year before. Whoever wrote that was not making an excuse for a trade that did not exist yet. Either I trade the Court's number for the yard book or I take it, and once it is taken this yard never opens its books to anyone from Soulrest again.

I gave Neeja-Xul the Court's number and she gave me her grandmother's book, and between the two of them the Cutters' defence is sound: they have made this worse and they did not start it. She asked me to say so somewhere it would be heard and I have not promised.
Harbourmaster Cuiro-Vaneth will let me read the outbound manifests for the last ten years for a hundred and fifty, which is a great deal of money for something he is telling me is public.

The manifests he gave me are the fair copies and they are short. The gem tonnage out of Archon has gone up five times over in ten years and the fair copies account for about a third of it. The rest is going out as something else or is not going out through his book at all.

The bonded store behind the crane has crates in it that are not in any manifest and the seals on them are not Imperial. They are a plain lead disc with a ring pressed into it and nobody on this quay will say whose it is. I counted the crates from the crane platform and nobody stopped me.

I have the true tonnage now and it does not do what I expected. Five times over in ten years is a great deal of gem and it is nothing at all against four hundred years of the Court's return column. Whatever is happening at Archon is a crime and a business and it is not the thing that started the curve. Three ways at the true tonnage and each one closes the other two: the crane crew will not talk to a man who has threatened their harbourmaster, and a store entered quietly cannot then be entered loudly.

The ring on the lead seals is the same ring the Blackwood Company's factors wear at Lilmoth. They are buying sap and gem both, at prices that only make sense if you believe the trees are dying and you want to be holding the stock when they do. I have seen that ring before and it took me two days to remember where.

I paid the hundred and fifty, read the fair copies, and got the rest by asking the crane crew who they load for after dark. The gem trade out of Archon is five times what it was and it cannot account for the curve. That is worth more than catching anybody.

Undersexton Bel Mourne is Rell's own second and she says the Ninth Recension is a forgery. Not an old one. She says the ninth clause was put into the fair copies in her lifetime and that she can show me who did it, and she wants me to hear it from her before I hear it from somebody who hates me.

Her argument is the ink and the paper stock and a gap of two clauses in three copies she has found in three houses. It is a good argument. She has been making it for eleven years and the Court has been not-answering it for eleven years, which she says is itself the answer. She made the whole argument to me in one morning without notes.

I put the seventh recension to her, the older one in the archive with the clause already in it in an older hand. She had seen it. She says the seventh is the one that was forged, and that the forgery is three hundred years old and was done for the same reason, which is that a Court with a claimant is a Court that can ask for things.

Neither of us can prove it. She cannot prove the clause was inserted and I cannot prove it was not, and the only person who has read every copy is an archivist who has spent thirty years declining to say. What she has proved is that Rell knows the argument exists, has known for eleven years, and read the clause at me anyway.

I have both arguments now and neither of them wins. What I am is either the thing a four-hundred-year-old book said would come or a thing an Undersexton needed to exist, and the useful part is that the sextons cannot tell either, and will act as though they can.

Ashul-Tei is a rootkeeper of the Deep-Kin and she has agreed to let me hear what the interior says about the tide, on the condition that I come without the Court's mark on me and that I do not write in her gallery.

The Deep-Kin's account is short. The coast is a wound. Foreigners drink and do not give back, the wells are being cut for sale by their own people at foreign prices, and the answer is to close the coast and let the interior alone. She says it without heat, the way you would describe a bad tooth. She said it to me without heat, the way you would describe a bad tooth.

Then she showed me a text they took off a body in the Deep Marshes eleven years ago. It is not a Deep-Kin text. It is a letter of instruction, in Jel, from something calling itself the Steward of the Count, and it is addressed to a keeper who had been managing an intake for it.

The letter is patient and it is not mad. It thanks the keeper for the year's work, it corrects a figure, and it explains, in three lines, that what is held is held so that the wells will give, and that this arrangement is older than the writer and was not the writer's idea. It signs itself Ixtu-Meer. I have now read the antagonist's case before I have met him and it is better than the Court's. She will let me carry the letter out or keep it in the gallery, not both, and once it has left Helstrom it never comes back.

Ashul-Tei has known the letter's contents for eleven years and has told nobody outside the gallery, because the Deep-Kin's whole argument is that foreigners are drinking the marsh, and the letter says the marsh has been drinking itself since before there were foreigners to blame. She told me that last, and only after I had read it.

I have heard the Deep-Kin's answer and read the Steward's own letter and remembered it, which is what she permitted. He writes like a clerk. He is holding something back from the roots on purpose, he thinks it is the arrangement that makes the wells work, and he did not begin it.

Rell has opened the crypt road to me. It goes from under the low chapel inland under the Stone Wastes and it is the only way to whatever is making that sound that does not involve digging. She has called in a favour with the mortuary to do it and she said so, which she has never done before.

The lit part of the road ends at the third gate. Beyond it the Court's own stonework stops and something older carries on, and the older work is better. The joints are tighter than anything standing above ground in this province. I stood at the third gate for a while before I went past it.

The road floods from below on a rhythm and the rhythm is the sound. Water comes up through the floor for the count of forty, holds, and goes back down, and it has been doing that since before the Court put a single stone down here. The mortuary hands walk it by the count and have for four hundred years and none of them have ever wondered what is doing the counting. I counted it out with them until I had the rhythm myself.

The old road does not go to a tomb. It goes to a gallery cut across the top of something enormous, and the enormous thing is worked stone, and it is running. I can feel it through the floor on the count of forty. This is a xanmeer and it is not a ruin.

There is a body in the gallery in Court robes that has been there perhaps ten years and its own book is under it. A sexton called Ivo Sarn came down here alone, wrote everything I have just worked out, and did not go back up. His last entry is a list of the intakes he had counted and the count is not finished. Sarn stays where he is or comes up with me. If I leave him the Court has only my word for the gallery, and if I bring him the gallery becomes a Court matter and stops being mine. Either the gallery stays a stranger's story or it becomes the Court's own sexton's, and taking one closes the other.

I have walked the crypt road to its end and stood on the gallery over the machine. It is a xanmeer built to hold, it is four thousand years old, it is running, and the rhythm the mortuary walks by is its rhythm. I came back up and told Rell and she sat down on the stair.

The intakes are where the machine takes. Six of them can be reached from the gallery walkway and one of those six has a gate that a person can move. If I close it I will find out whether the wells above are fed by this thing or merely near it, and the well above the sixth intake is the one on the Soulrest stair.

Rell says the Court cannot authorise it and cannot stop me and would like the result. Bel Mourne says that if I am right about what the intake does then somebody will die of it, and that she would still do it, and that I should be clear with myself about which of those two sentences I am acting on.
The gate is closed. The machine's rhythm did not change. Nothing down here noticed at all. I closed it myself and then I sat on the walkway and waited.

The Soulrest well went cold within the day. Sap in the basin, right colour, does nothing, exactly as at the Bone Ladder. So it is not that the machine is stealing what the wells should get. It is that the wells are drinking what the machine lets past. The sapwells work because of the thing that is killing the marsh, and I have just proved it by turning it off. One gate, one test, and whichever way I run it is the way it was run. A proof taken on paper cannot then be taken with a hand, and a well that has gone cold does not un-go cold because I changed my mind about the method.

A mortuary hand called Sesh-Weth died on the second day with the gate shut, in the ordinary way, of a chest thing he had had for years. The well did not take him. He is the only person in four hundred years of that book who went into the Soulrest ground and gave nothing back, and it is written next to my name because Ojal-Weeth writes down who was there.

I opened the gate again on the second day and the Soulrest well came back within the hour. I know what the machine does now and it cost one man who was going to die anyway and who deserved better than to be an experiment. I have written his name down here because there is nowhere else it will be written.

Hosk-Vei says the Recension does not mean that the count will be read by somebody who is owed nothing. It means the count will be read by somebody who is put into it. There is a basin on the gallery and to read what is held below I have to let the thing below hold me.

He was clear about the cost and I want it written down that he was clear. Whatever is in that basin will take my pattern and keep it, and there is no rootkeeper, no sexton, no cure and no ending that takes it back out. He said it three times and then he asked me not to decide today.
Bel Mourne says do not. Rell says it is what I am for. Ashul-Tei's question, the one she made me repeat, was for the writer of that letter, and I cannot ask it of him without going in.

I have put my hand in the basin at the seventh bay. It is cold and it is not sap. Something read me, all the way through, in about the time it takes to lose your footing, and the count of forty went out of rhythm for one cycle and came back. I am in the Count now. I do not feel changed and I am told that is normal and that it is not the same as being unchanged. There is no second reading and no other basin. What was done at the seventh bay closes every other way of doing it, and there is nothing anywhere in this province that undoes it.

What being in it gets me is that the machine now answers when I put my hand on it. Not in words. It gives me the shape of what it is holding, the way a ledger gives you a total, and the total is four thousand years of everything that has died in this province and did not get down to a root.

The other thing being in it gets me is that I cannot be re-issued clean any more. The wells still take me and what comes back is a little further from what went in each time. Hosk-Vei knew that would happen. He told me the cost and he did not tell me that part, and when I asked him why not he said that nobody who was told that part has ever gone in.

I am in the Count. It cost what I was told it would cost and one thing I was not told, and it is the only reason anything after this is possible. I have written the date down. Nobody else is going to.

Neeja-Xul says there is another way at the machine and it does not involve the Court at all. Every intake it has runs on live root. Cut the root above the intake with a proper skei and the intake stops, and eleven of them can be reached from below without ever going onto the Court's gallery. She told me how and then told me she would not come with me.

She is not offering this as a kindness. The Cutters have been blamed for thirty years for a thing they did not start and she would like the province to watch somebody cut a root for a reason it cannot argue with. She was honest about that, which I did not expect and which does not make it a better idea.

The knife is under the reed-walk in the flooded chamber. It is her grandmother's and it is the reason her grandmother's yard book exists, and she will not go in for it herself because she is afraid of what the yard would think of her for wanting it. She will not go in for it and she asked me whether I would.

I have the skei. What it opens is a route to the machine that goes under the Court, past the sextons, past the Recension and past whatever I am supposed to be, and cuts eleven live roots to get there. Everyone I have asked agrees this would stop the intakes. Nobody I have asked will say what stopping them does to the wells above, and I have already proved what stopping one does. The knife is hers or it is mine. If I keep it the route under the Court opens and the yard is owed something it will collect; if I hand it back the route closes, and it is the only door in this whole business that opens again if I ask.

I told Neeja-Xul I would not carry her grandmother's knife to use as an argument and I brought it up out of the water and put it in her hand instead. She held it for a long time. The route under the Court is still there and I know where it starts, and I do not have the thing that opens it.

Sesh-Anaat has sent for me by a route I do not understand — a carter at Nine-Mud knew my name and knew where I had been, and had been told at a well two days from here. The rootkeeper at Thorn says the tree has asked for me. She says trees do not do this.

The causeway out to the tree takes most of a morning and there is nothing on it. Sesh-Anaat walked it with me and did not say anything for the whole of it, and at the end she said that in forty years the tree at Thorn has spoken plainly twice, and that both times it was because it had run out of other things to do.

The tree spoke to me and it was not a dream and there was no ceremony. It said four sentences. It said that what is below Soulrest is not its enemy and never was. It said the arrangement is older than any tree standing in this province. It said that the roots have been drinking an allowance for four thousand years and have forgotten how to drink anything else. And it said: do not ask me what to do.

I asked it anyway, three times, in three different ways. It did not answer and it did not go away, and Sesh-Anaat stood in the water and cried, quietly, because a tree that will not answer a question it invited you out here to ask is a tree that does not know.

Sesh-Anaat says I must not repeat the fourth sentence to any rootkeeper in the province. The first three are theology and can be argued with. The fourth is the tree admitting it has no instruction, and she says that if that gets out, the interior will do something and it will not be a considered something. The fourth sentence is kept or it is carried, and once it has been said out loud to anyone it can never again be a thing only three of us heard.

Four sentences from a tree, and the fourth of them was that it does not know. Everyone from here on will tell me what the Hist wants. I have heard what the Hist wants and it is for somebody else to decide.
The Court will not open its own crypt road to a machine it has not voted on. Nine sextons, and I need five of them, and Rell has one vote and a great deal of opinion about the other eight.

Four are Rell's already. Two will not move for anything I have. The three in the middle are a Lilmoth sexton who wants the Court out of Lilmoth, an old woman who has read the Recension in four copies and believes none of them, and a man who is in debt to the Wet Ledger for eleven hundred.

The old woman asked me one question, which was whether I thought the ninth clause was written for me. I said I did not know. She said that was the first honest answer she had had out of anyone in the chapter room in eleven years and voted with me.

The man in debt can be bought, which costs eleven hundred, or his debt can be read out, which ruins him and gets his vote and loses me the two who were never going to move plus one who was. Rell would prefer I bought him. Rell would prefer a great many things she has not said out loud.

Five of nine. The Court stands with me and the crypt road is open to the gallery for as long as this chapter sits. Rell counted the hands twice and then went and stood by the water marks on the wall for a while.

The Wet Ledger owns the river freight and every barge that could carry what will have to come out of the Stone Wastes. Ruvela Sath will put it to the compact for me and she has been clear that the compact does not vote on theology and will not be asked to.

Their objection is not superstition and I was wrong to expect it to be. Eleven of the nineteen have money in gem freight out of Archon. If the province decides the gem trade is what killed the tide, they are ruined, and they would rather it were the Cutters or the machine or anything at all.

Which is convenient, because it is not the gem trade, and I can prove it. The tonnage out of Archon is five times what it was and it is nothing against four hundred years of return column. I came in expecting to fight these people and what I actually have is the only exoneration they are ever going to get.

Sath wants the exoneration and does not want it read out with the true tonnage attached, because the true tonnage is a crime even if it is not the crime. Either the compact hears the whole arithmetic or it hears the half that helps it, and the half that helps it is a lie that happens to be true. She put it to me as a courtesy and it was not one.

I read the whole arithmetic to eleven factors in a warehouse — the return column, the tonnage, the dates, all of it. They are exonerated of the thing that matters and indicted for the thing that does not, and they voted with me anyway because the arithmetic was in the Court's own hand with Hosk-Vei's name under mine.

The Deep-Kin do not have a vote to win. They have eleven rootkeepers at eleven wells and a consensus that forms when enough of them stop objecting, and Ashul-Tei says that if I want it I will have to walk to them, all of them, and that she will not send ahead.

Seven of the eleven will not object if the interior is not opened to Court traffic. Two object to me personally, being an outlander with a Court name. Two object to the whole idea on the grounds that a foreigner reading the Count is exactly what the Court would want them to believe is prophecy.

The two who object to the idea are not wrong and I did not try to tell them they were. I gave them Bel Mourne's copies with the gap in them and let them read the Court's own argument against its own text.

The last two want a price and the price is not gold. They want the crypt road sealed behind me when it is done, so that whatever is under the Wastes stays a thing the Court has to walk two days to reach. That is a promise I can make and would then have to keep in the last hour of this. Four ways to a consensus that does not object, and each one closes the rest: an interior told the fourth sentence cannot then be walked to over nineteen days, and a keeper's name spent is spent.

Nobody objects any more. I walked to eleven wells in nineteen days and gave two of them the Court's own doubt to read and promised two of them the road would be sealed after, and the interior has stopped objecting, which is the only kind of yes it gives.

Nobody can get to the intakes from below without cutters. Eleven live roots, all of them in water, and there are four yards in this province that know how to open one without killing it. Neeja-Xul speaks for one of them. I have four yards to find and one season to do it in.

Mudwater and Salt-Egg will come if Blackrose comes. The fourth yard is at Lilmoth and it is not a yard, it is two brothers and a Blackwood Company retainer, and they have been paid a year in advance for something they will not describe. I went to the fourth yard without her name on me, as she told me to.

The Company has bought the Lilmoth cutters to be ready to cut on its own account, which only makes sense if somebody has told the Company what is under the Wastes. Somebody has. There are five people who could have and I have been talking to all of them. The Lilmoth yard is shown to the others as bought, or bought back quietly, or gone round entirely on my own standing — never two of those, because the first makes the second pointless and the third makes both unnecessary. Whichever of the three I take closes the other two, and none of them can be tried after another has failed.

Three yards, and the fourth stood down when I put the Company's retainer in front of the other three and let them look at him. Cutters are not sentimental about each other and they are extremely sentimental about being sold.

The Prefect can issue a writ of works. Without it the whole business is an unlicensed excavation on Imperial-chartered ground and everyone who lifts a stone for me is liable. He has not said no. He has said what a writ of works normally requires and it is a list of four things I do not have.

What he wants is not on the list. Stormhold has two cohorts on paper and one in fact, because the reserves went to Vvardenfell, and the Prefect has been writing to the Governor at Gideon about it for two years. He wants the province's other powers on a piece of paper agreeing that the Empire is needed for something. He told me this himself, once I stopped pretending not to have noticed.

So the writ is not about the machine. The writ is a lever he is using me to pull on a governor two hundred leagues of bad road away. He was completely open about it once I stopped pretending not to have noticed, and he is not ashamed of it, and it is still the cheapest thing anybody in this act has asked me for.

The writ of works is signed and sealed and it cost me nothing but a paragraph, which the Prefect wrote himself and I put my name to, saying that the province's powers have asked the Empire for its help. He will send it to Gideon by the fast boat.

Whatever comes out of the Wastes has to be carried by hands, and the hands in this province are on Weeja-Sen's list at Lilmoth. She will hire out sixty for the work. She wants to know what the work is and she has already been told a version of it by somebody else. She wants to know what the work is and I have to decide how much of it to tell her.

The Blackwood Company got here first. Their factor has offered her list double for the same season and will not say what for, and she has not taken it, and she has not refused it either, and she is doing that on purpose in front of me.

Her price is not gold and she said so straight away. Eleven of her people went into the rotting quarter over the last two winters on Company hire and did not come out, and nobody in Lilmoth will go in after them because there is a Hist in there and its rootkeepers do not acknowledge that the Empire exists, let alone a dockmaster. She told me the price and then waited to see whether I would ask what was in the quarter.

So the wharf's voice costs a walk into the rotting quarter to find out what happened to eleven people. I can do that, or I can outbid a trading company with more money than the province, or I can hire the list as a Dockhand and let the list decide for itself, which it will do badly and in my favour. Weeja-Sen asked for eleven names. If I answer with coin instead she takes the coin, and she does not ask again, and the eleven stay where they are for good. Answering her with coin closes the naming, and answering with names closes the buying, and neither is offered twice.

Eleven names, and I brought back what happened to nine of them, which is that the Company had them cutting inside the rotting quarter and the rootkeepers in there stopped them the way rootkeepers do. Weeja-Sen read the nine names out on the wharf at first light and the list is mine and the Company will not hire in Lilmoth again this year.

Eleven live roots have to be opened to reach the intakes from below and only the rootkeepers can give leave for that. What I am asking Sesh-Anaat for is the thing her order exists to refuse. She heard the whole of it without interrupting and then stood in the water for a long time.

The keepers' answer is a rite and not a vote. Leave to open a live root is given by three keepers standing at the root, and it has been given eleven times in four hundred years, and every one of the eleven is written down with the reason and whether the reason held. She read me the rite before she would hear what I wanted it for.

She read me the eleven. Nine of them were for water. One was for a road. One was in the year the Knahaten Flu came out of Stormhold and it is the only one where the reason is written as: we did not know what else to do.

She will stand for it herself and she needs two more keepers and the two nearest are the ones who will ask what the tree at Thorn told me. If I answer that honestly the leave will not be given by anyone. If I do not answer it, the leave is given on a silence, and the silence will be in the book next to my name for four hundred years. The leave is given on the true reason, on a silence, or on a technicality, and whichever it is goes into the book in ink and is read by keepers for four hundred years. There is no second asking. Each of the three closes the other two the moment it is written in the book, and the book is never again opened at that page.

Three keepers stood at the root at Thorn and gave leave for eleven, and the reason written in the book is the true one, which is that the wells are drinking an allowance and nobody knows what happens when it stops. Sesh-Anaat wrote it in her own hand and put my name under hers.

Neloth Vaun is the Dres salt-factor at Archon and he holds the deep-water berth. He has heard the whole business already and he does not care about the tide, the Court, the trees or me. He cares that eleven cutters and sixty hands are about to be in one place under Imperial writ, and he wants to know what that does to the price of stock.

He wants a clause. He wants it written into the writ of works that the labour engaged is engaged by contract and is not therefore available for any other purpose, which sounds like nothing and means that sixty free Argonians working under an Imperial writ cannot be taken by a Dres raiding party, and he wants that because a raid on a lawful Imperial works is the one thing that would bring the cohorts back to this province. He put the wording in front of me and waited while I read it twice.

The clause protects sixty people who would otherwise be exactly the stock his House takes. He is asking for it to protect his House's freedom to keep taking everyone else, by keeping the Legion out. It is the best thing anyone has offered me in this act and the reason for it is the worst. The clause is signed or it is not. If I sign it, sixty people are safe for a season and House Dres has its year; if I refuse it and buy the water, the sixty are not safe and Vaun has my name. I cannot have the berth and the refusal both. Signing closes the refusal and refusing closes the signing; I cannot have the berth on both terms and nobody in the compound will pretend otherwise.

The clause is in the writ and the berth is open. Sixty people who would have been stock are, for one season, not, and House Dres has bought itself another year of the Legion staying in Vvardenfell, and I signed that.

Eight voices, and they are all in. There is a works camp at the Bone Ladder with sixty hands, four cutting yards, the Ledger's barges at the Archon end and an Imperial writ nailed to a post, and none of it can go down until the eleven roots are opened and the shaft is shored, and that is a fortnight of ordinary work. I did not build any of it and it is mine to answer for.

The camp has become a place. There is a cook fire the Deep-Kin keepers will not sit at and a second one they will, and a bonded store for the writ's paperwork, and a sick-tent, and somebody has cut a step into the rib so that Teeja-Lun does not have to climb. Nobody planned any of that. I have been walking through it every evening and counting who is still here.

The eleventh root would not open. Three keepers stood at it for two days and it would not, and on the third morning it had opened itself in the night, which Sesh-Anaat says has never happened and which she will not discuss further. I was not there when it opened and neither was anyone else.

The Blackwood Company's people are here. Not hiding — camped, on the far side of the rib, with a writ of their own out of Leyawiin that says nothing about the Stone Wastes and looks impressive at a distance. Their factor sent a jar of Cyrodiilic wine over with a note asking to be told when we go down. The Company's camp is left where it is or it is opened up, and once I have their factor in my tent they know exactly who I am, which closes the possibility of going down without them knowing.

Teeja-Lun asked me, at her own well, in front of the whole camp, whether I was going to put the Bone Ladder out. She has kept a wound open with a knife for eleven days for people who walk past her. I said I did not know what opening the Count does to the wells. She said that she knew that, and that she had asked anyway, and that I should remember she asked.

The shaft is shored and the eleven are open and the way down is walkable. Fifteen days. The camp is still standing and the Company's camp is still standing beside it, and tomorrow I go down and I have written tonight's date here because I do not think I will be writing much for a while.

Below the eleventh root the water stops and there is a dry gallery under the Wastes with grey dust on the floor of it, ankle deep, that is not dust. It is what four thousand years of held pattern leaves behind when it is held too long. Bel Mourne came down with me and would not walk in it.

There are people down here. Not many and not soldiers. They keep the intakes, they are extremely old, they have been re-issued so many times that Bel Mourne says they are barely the same people, and they are not surprised to see us. One of them has been expecting a tally-reader for a hundred and forty years and told me so as though we had an appointment.

Two ways on. The counting floor is long and lit and there are eleven keepers on it who will each want to say something. The intake stair is shorter and goes through the working parts of the machine, where the wards are still live and the thing that has been sitting in the third bay since the Duskfall is still sitting in it. I stood at the fork for longer than I would like to admit.

The keeper in the fifth bay is called Ei-Vashan and she wants to leave. She has kept the fifth intake for two hundred years and she has worked out, on her own, from her own count, roughly what I have come to do, and she would like to be above ground when it happens. Nobody down here has ever left.

The thing in the third bay is not a keeper and is not a guard. It was put there. It does not follow and it does not leave the bay and if you go through the bay it will do what it was left there to do, and there is a corridor round it that adds an hour and that everybody down here uses. I asked what it was and nobody down here would give me a word for it.

I took the counting floor and heard eleven keepers out, one at a time, which took a day and a half. Not one of them argued with me. They told me what their bay does and how long they have kept it and, most of them, what year they think it is.

Ixtu-Meer is a very old Argonian in a room with a chair in it and he stood up when I came in. He said that he had read the letter I am carrying, because he wrote it, and asked whether Ashul-Tei was well. Then he asked what I wanted to know and said that we had time, which under the circumstances was a strange thing to find comforting.

He does not deny anything. The reservoir holds what the roots do not get. It has held it since before the Duskfall. He did not build it, he does not know who did, and he took the work over from a keeper called Vei-Anaat who took it from someone else, and the chain of them is written on the wall of the chamber and it is long. He answered everything I put to him and did not once ask what I intended.

His case, as he put it: the wells give because he lets an allowance past. He showed me the ledger of it. It is the same arithmetic I did in the Court's archive from the other end, and it comes out the same, and I did mine first and he did not know I had done it.

Three things he is right about, and I checked all three myself before I met him. The curve is older than the cutting; I read that in the Tally. The wells drink what the machine lets past; I proved that with my own hand on the sixth intake and a man is buried for it. The gem trade cannot account for the curve; I counted the tonnage at Archon. He did not tell me any of these. He asked me what I had found and then agreed with it.

What he will not say is why it is filling now rather than holding. He says the answer is that it was always filling and the difference is that the province has grown enough to notice, and I do not believe him, and he knows I do not, and he did not try again.

He asked me a question and I have written it down because I have not been able to stop turning it over. He asked: whose count are you? Somebody is keeping one on you, he said, and you have never once asked who, and he is right and I do not know the answer.

I asked him Ashul-Tei's question, the one I was made to say back twice: what does the marsh owe you. He was quiet for a while and then he said that this is the only question anyone has brought him in four hundred years that was not about the machine, and he answered it, and the answer is his and I am not going to write it here.

There is a way to open it that does not involve killing him and he told me what it is himself, unprompted, in detail, twice, because he would rather I did it properly than badly. He would still prefer I did not do it. Both of those were true at the same time in the same voice and I have met priests who could not manage that.

He has not asked me not to. He has asked me to be able to say, afterwards, what I thought would happen, and to be wrong in a way that I chose rather than in a way I drifted into. That is the whole of his request and he made it once.

We talked for most of a day. I know how the Count opens, I know what he thinks it will do, I know what the keepers on the floor below think it will do, and the three accounts do not agree. Nobody is going to settle this for me and he was the last person who might have.

The reservoir floor is down eleven steps through the arch. There is a stone sill across the bottom of the arch, ankle high, worn in the middle. Ixtu-Meer said that everyone who has gone over it has come back up, and that he has never been able to work out whether that is because it lets them or because none of them did anything. I have been standing on this side of it for most of an hour.

Ei-Vashan told me at the Bone Ladder well, three weeks ago, that once the working parts have your weight on the floor they will not accept a hand on the intakes from above any more. She said it as an ordinary fact about her job. It is the only warning anybody gave me and it was given before I knew what it was about.

The camp knew before I did. Rell has moved the barges to the deep-water berth and the cutters have stopped work on the twelfth root and the sick-tent has been struck. Nobody told them to. They have all read the same thing off the same fortnight and they are behaving like people who expect the road to close behind somebody.

The Court's chapter has been sitting for four days over whether the crypt road stays open after. The Deep-Kin have withdrawn to the eleventh root. Weeja-Sen has paid off thirty of the sixty and sent them home with the season's money, which is not what a dockmaster does when she expects the work to continue. None of them has said any of this to me.

I am standing on the near side of the sill. Everything above me stops being reachable when I put my weight on the other side of it: the crypt road, the intakes from above, the camp, the eight voices and whatever any of them still owed me. Nobody has said this. I have worked it out from a keeper's remark and a dockmaster paying people off, which is how I have found out everything else in this business.
I stepped over it. It is a stone about as high as my ankle and it took less than a second and nothing happened at all.

The floor of the reservoir is a room the size of a settlement and it is nearly dark and the sluice gear at the end of it was built to be worked by one pair of hands. He came down after me and did not try to stop me and stood where I could see him.

Four ways out of this room, and I have been told about all four by people who disagreed about every one of them. Open it. Keep it and take his place. Kill him and let the working parts run untended until they stop. Or go back up the eleven steps, which is a thing I can physically do and which nobody has offered as an answer. Each of the four closes the other three the moment it is begun.

I opened the Count. Four thousand years of held pattern went down into the root water in about two hours and the roots took what they could and the rest went past them into the dark, and the wells in this province will never work the way they did. Ixtu-Meer sat down on the steps while it happened and did not watch. Afterwards he thanked me, which I had not expected and did not want.

It is done and I am still here and it is the eleventh of Sun's Height. There is no ceremony and nobody has come to find me. The Bone Ladder well is doing whatever it is now going to do and Teeja-Lun is sitting beside it finding out, the same as everyone else.

The things people say to me now are all different and none of them are about prophecy. A carter asked whether the coast road is safe. A sexton asked what I want done with the ninth chair. Ojal-Weeth asked whether Sesh-Weth's name should go in the book as a burial or as something else and I did not have an answer for her either.

There are eleven things in this journal I never finished. The two of Weeja-Sen's people who were never accounted for. Whoever told the Blackwood Company. Why the eleventh root opened itself in the night. Why the tree at Thorn asked for me. Nobody is going to come and close any of them and the province has gone back to being a place with weather.

I have walked from Soulrest to Stormhold and back to see what changed, which took eighteen days, and the honest answer is that most of it did not. What changed is at the wells and in eleven specific rooms, and everywhere else the reeds are doing what reeds do. I can walk the province asking, or I can kneel at the Ladder and find out on my own skin, and the first answer I get is the one I will believe, so it matters which I do first. Walking it first closes the other, because whichever answer I get first is the one that stands.

I have been to nine wells and four settlements and asked people what they think happened. Nobody agrees. Two of them think it was somebody else. One of them thinks nothing happened and that the Court made all of it up, and I could not prove otherwise to him in an afternoon and I did try.

topics_known: the ninth clause of the Drowned Tally

journal.text: Undersexton Aveline Rell has given me a sealed quarterly return to carry from Soulrest to the Court's factor in Gideon. She pays a hundred and twenty in advance, which is more than the work is worth, and she asked twice whether anyone had spoken to me on the stair.

The seal on the return is a mortuary seal and it is not fresh. Whatever is in it was closed up before I was hired. At the Bone Ladder the keeper asked me whose count I was carrying and would not say what she meant.
A man in a good coat walked the coast track behind me from the Ladder to Hollow-Reeds and turned back when I stopped to sit. He was not a carter and he was not going to Gideon.

The Court's factor in Gideon opened the return in front of me and read three lines of it and stopped. He said the Undersexton knows what is in her own quarterlies and did not need me to bring her one. I was not carrying a book. I was carrying a man in a good coat, from Soulrest to Gideon, to see who he was.

The factor's name for the man in the coat is Sedd Ravano and he takes money from the Wet Ledger to know what the Court is writing down. The factor says this is neither news nor a secret and that Rell has been trying to put a face to it for two seasons. I have written the name down because I do not trust myself to remember it in four days.

I put the return in the factor's hand in Gideon and said nothing about the man in the coat, and I was paid the rest of my hundred and twenty. Rell wrote something down when I told her the road had been quiet, and she did not believe me, and she hired me again anyway.

Rell wants eleven burial boxes counted and their weights written down. They came back from the wells at Bone Ladder and Salt-Egg Camp with nothing in them, which she says happens, and which she is nonetheless paying me to write down.

All eleven are empty and all eleven are the right weight for empty. The mortuary hands say the bodies went into the wells and did not come out as anything, not as sap, not as heat, not as the smell they expect. One of them would not go on talking about it inside. I weighed all eleven myself.

I sat on the burial stair after dark and there is a sound under the Stone Wastes. It is not surf and it is not wind in the salt-store. It is regular, and slow, and it has been going on longer than anyone in Soulrest has been paying attention to it.

The mortuary hand's name is Ojal-Weeth and outside, where the sound is, she said the boxes have been coming back empty for longer than eleven. She has been counting them herself since her mother died and it is not eleven, it is closer to ninety. I went outside with her because she would not say it in the shed.

Eleven boxes, eleven weights, all of them the weight of an empty box. Rell read the list twice and put it in a press that already had a great many lists in it. I gave her the list and she did not thank me for it.

Rell wants to know why the sapwell at the Bone Ladder has stopped giving. She is not sending a rootkeeper and she is not sending a sexton. She is sending me, because I owe the wells nothing and because whatever is wrong there will not have any hold on me.

The basin at the Ladder is full and the sap in it is the right colour and it does not do anything. Teeja-Lun has put her hand in it every morning for eleven days and the root has not tasted her. She has been keeping the wound open with a knife because she is afraid it will close. I put my own hand in the basin and nothing tasted me either.

Teeja-Lun says the well did not fail slowly. It gave one night and did not give the next, and the night it stopped was the night the carters heard the Wastes go quiet. Not loud. Quiet. I asked her twice and she gave me the same night both times.

Under the rib there is a shaft in the stone that is older than the road and it is not a burial. The sap in the basin is not standing still. It is going down, slowly, into something, and it has been going down since the night it stopped coming back. Whatever I do at this basin closes the others: a wound cut wider cannot be reported as a wound left alone, and a keeper protected cannot also be a keeper contradicted.

Teeja-Lun has known about the shaft her whole life. Every keeper on this coast knows. They do not speak about it because a well that drains is still a well, and a keeper who says otherwise is a keeper nobody kneels to. She told me this after I had already found it, which I notice.

I told Rell the well at the Ladder is not empty, it is draining, and that there is a shaft under the rib that the keepers have known about for generations. She did not write it down straight away. She sat with it.

Rell says I am becoming legible. A stranger who does nothing but errands for the Drowned Court is a stranger everyone can read, and she would rather I were harder to read than that. She wants me to take a name somewhere else — any name, she does not care which — so that when I am seen on a road there is another reason for it.

She was clear about one thing and I think she meant it. Whatever I swear to, she says, the Court will still have me, and if I swear to nothing the Court will still have me, and it will only cost me more later. She would not say what it would cost.
I have a name in the Wet Ledger now and a reason to be on the river that is not the Court's reason. Rell asked which one I had taken and then did not write it down, which I noticed.
Rell has sent for me to stand in the Court's chapter room while something is read out. She would not say what. She would only say that I should not answer anything anybody asks me until it is over.

The Ninth Recension of the Drowned Tally is a text the Court has been copying for four hundred years, and one clause of it was read out at me. When the tide fails, it says, the count will be read by one who is owed nothing — not of the marsh, not of the Court, and holding no debt to any root. Then everyone in the room looked at me.

I asked Rell afterwards whether she believed it. She said that what she believes is not the useful question, and that the useful question is whether the sextons believe it, and that they do, and that this is worth more than either of us being right.

The chapter room copy is in a hand I have seen before. It is the same hand as the fair copies Rell's own clerks make, and the ink on the ninth clause does not match the ink on the eighth. That proves the clause was copied later than the rest of the book. It does not prove it was invented.

There is an older recension in the Court's archive, the seventh, and the clause is in that one too, in an older hand, worded differently and meaning the same. So either the forgery is four hundred years old or it is not a forgery. I asked the archivist which and he said that this is the question the Court has been arguing about for four hundred years and that nobody has ever won it.

I stood there and let them read it and said nothing, and afterwards the Court has a tally-reader and I have a name I did not ask for. Rell says the name is worth more than the money and she is not wrong, and I notice that she never said whether it is true.

Hosk-Vei has agreed to open the Tally to me, all four hundred years of it, on the condition that I read it in the room and write nothing down that I cannot say out loud to him first. He wants the same thing I want, which is a number.

The Tally is a burial book. Every death the Court handled, what was paid, and what the wells gave back afterwards, in the Court's own units, four hundred years without a gap. It is the only continuous record of the tide in the province and nobody outside this room has ever added it up. I have been given the whole of it to read.

Adding it up took eleven days. The return per death is flat from the earliest volumes until the year thirty-nine of the third era's fourth century, and from that year it falls, and it has not stopped falling since. It is not a cliff. It is a curve, and the curve is thirty-six years old. I did the addition myself and I checked it twice.

The first licence to cut a sapwell for sale was granted in the year forty-seven. The curve begins in thirty-nine. Whatever the Sap-Cutters have done to this province, and they have done a great deal, the tide was already going before the first of them picked up a knife. I looked the licence date up before I let myself believe the rest of it.

In the older volumes there is a hand that is not a sexton's, entering corrections in the margins, always to the return column and always downward. Hosk-Vei says the Court calls that hand the Steward of the Count, and that it has been appearing in the margins of this book since the fourth volume, and that the fourth volume is three hundred and ten years old. Hosk-Vei will let me leave with the sum in my head or with it in his archive under both our names, and not both, because a fair copy is a thing the Court has said and a memory is a thing only I have.

The name in the fourth volume is Ixtu-Meer. Hosk-Vei says it is a title and not a person, the way Undersexton is a title, and then he said that if I found a sexton who had ever met a second one he would like to be told.

The curve is thirty-six years old and the cutting licences are twenty-eight. I can say that now and mean it, and I can say who has been writing corrections into the return column since before anyone alive was born. Hosk-Vei asked me to say it out loud to him twice before he would let me leave with it.

Neeja-Xul cuts sapwells for money and does not pretend otherwise. She has agreed to show me the yard and the books that go with it on one condition, which is that I bring her whatever number the Court has, because nobody has ever told the Cutters what they are supposed to have done.

The yard's own ledger goes back twenty-eight years to the first licence. Two hundred and forty wells cut, of which the yard has records of eighty still giving and sixty-one closed. That is a great deal of harm and it is not four hundred years of anything. She let me count the yard's own entries without standing over me.

Neeja-Xul says the thing nobody will hear: the wells the Cutters opened are the only wells on the coast that still give at all, because a fresh wound gives before it learns better. She thinks this is an argument. It is also, as far as I can tell, true, and it is the worst true thing I have been told this season.

Her grandmother's yard book is under the bench and it is older than the licence. The Cutters were cutting before the Empire gave anyone leave to, back into the forties, and the earliest entry in it complains that the wells that year gave less than the year before. Whoever wrote that was not making an excuse for a trade that did not exist yet. Either I trade the Court's number for the yard book or I take it, and once it is taken this yard never opens its books to anyone from Soulrest again.

I gave Neeja-Xul the Court's number and she gave me her grandmother's book, and between the two of them the Cutters' defence is sound: they have made this worse and they did not start it. She asked me to say so somewhere it would be heard and I have not promised.
Harbourmaster Cuiro-Vaneth will let me read the outbound manifests for the last ten years for a hundred and fifty, which is a great deal of money for something he is telling me is public.

The manifests he gave me are the fair copies and they are short. The gem tonnage out of Archon has gone up five times over in ten years and the fair copies account for about a third of it. The rest is going out as something else or is not going out through his book at all.

The bonded store behind the crane has crates in it that are not in any manifest and the seals on them are not Imperial. They are a plain lead disc with a ring pressed into it and nobody on this quay will say whose it is. I counted the crates from the crane platform and nobody stopped me.

I have the true tonnage now and it does not do what I expected. Five times over in ten years is a great deal of gem and it is nothing at all against four hundred years of the Court's return column. Whatever is happening at Archon is a crime and a business and it is not the thing that started the curve. Three ways at the true tonnage and each one closes the other two: the crane crew will not talk to a man who has threatened their harbourmaster, and a store entered quietly cannot then be entered loudly.

The ring on the lead seals is the same ring the Blackwood Company's factors wear at Lilmoth. They are buying sap and gem both, at prices that only make sense if you believe the trees are dying and you want to be holding the stock when they do. I have seen that ring before and it took me two days to remember where.

I paid the hundred and fifty, read the fair copies, and got the rest by asking the crane crew who they load for after dark. The gem trade out of Archon is five times what it was and it cannot account for the curve. That is worth more than catching anybody.

Undersexton Bel Mourne is Rell's own second and she says the Ninth Recension is a forgery. Not an old one. She says the ninth clause was put into the fair copies in her lifetime and that she can show me who did it, and she wants me to hear it from her before I hear it from somebody who hates me.

Her argument is the ink and the paper stock and a gap of two clauses in three copies she has found in three houses. It is a good argument. She has been making it for eleven years and the Court has been not-answering it for eleven years, which she says is itself the answer. She made the whole argument to me in one morning without notes.

I put the seventh recension to her, the older one in the archive with the clause already in it in an older hand. She had seen it. She says the seventh is the one that was forged, and that the forgery is three hundred years old and was done for the same reason, which is that a Court with a claimant is a Court that can ask for things.

Neither of us can prove it. She cannot prove the clause was inserted and I cannot prove it was not, and the only person who has read every copy is an archivist who has spent thirty years declining to say. What she has proved is that Rell knows the argument exists, has known for eleven years, and read the clause at me anyway.

I have both arguments now and neither of them wins. What I am is either the thing a four-hundred-year-old book said would come or a thing an Undersexton needed to exist, and the useful part is that the sextons cannot tell either, and will act as though they can.

Ashul-Tei is a rootkeeper of the Deep-Kin and she has agreed to let me hear what the interior says about the tide, on the condition that I come without the Court's mark on me and that I do not write in her gallery.

The Deep-Kin's account is short. The coast is a wound. Foreigners drink and do not give back, the wells are being cut for sale by their own people at foreign prices, and the answer is to close the coast and let the interior alone. She says it without heat, the way you would describe a bad tooth. She said it to me without heat, the way you would describe a bad tooth.

Then she showed me a text they took off a body in the Deep Marshes eleven years ago. It is not a Deep-Kin text. It is a letter of instruction, in Jel, from something calling itself the Steward of the Count, and it is addressed to a keeper who had been managing an intake for it.

The letter is patient and it is not mad. It thanks the keeper for the year's work, it corrects a figure, and it explains, in three lines, that what is held is held so that the wells will give, and that this arrangement is older than the writer and was not the writer's idea. It signs itself Ixtu-Meer. I have now read the antagonist's case before I have met him and it is better than the Court's. She will let me carry the letter out or keep it in the gallery, not both, and once it has left Helstrom it never comes back.

Ashul-Tei has known the letter's contents for eleven years and has told nobody outside the gallery, because the Deep-Kin's whole argument is that foreigners are drinking the marsh, and the letter says the marsh has been drinking itself since before there were foreigners to blame. She told me that last, and only after I had read it.

I have heard the Deep-Kin's answer and read the Steward's own letter and remembered it, which is what she permitted. He writes like a clerk. He is holding something back from the roots on purpose, he thinks it is the arrangement that makes the wells work, and he did not begin it.

Rell has opened the crypt road to me. It goes from under the low chapel inland under the Stone Wastes and it is the only way to whatever is making that sound that does not involve digging. She has called in a favour with the mortuary to do it and she said so, which she has never done before.

The lit part of the road ends at the third gate. Beyond it the Court's own stonework stops and something older carries on, and the older work is better. The joints are tighter than anything standing above ground in this province. I stood at the third gate for a while before I went past it.

The road floods from below on a rhythm and the rhythm is the sound. Water comes up through the floor for the count of forty, holds, and goes back down, and it has been doing that since before the Court put a single stone down here. The mortuary hands walk it by the count and have for four hundred years and none of them have ever wondered what is doing the counting. I counted it out with them until I had the rhythm myself.

The old road does not go to a tomb. It goes to a gallery cut across the top of something enormous, and the enormous thing is worked stone, and it is running. I can feel it through the floor on the count of forty. This is a xanmeer and it is not a ruin.

There is a body in the gallery in Court robes that has been there perhaps ten years and its own book is under it. A sexton called Ivo Sarn came down here alone, wrote everything I have just worked out, and did not go back up. His last entry is a list of the intakes he had counted and the count is not finished. Sarn stays where he is or comes up with me. If I leave him the Court has only my word for the gallery, and if I bring him the gallery becomes a Court matter and stops being mine. Either the gallery stays a stranger's story or it becomes the Court's own sexton's, and taking one closes the other.

I have walked the crypt road to its end and stood on the gallery over the machine. It is a xanmeer built to hold, it is four thousand years old, it is running, and the rhythm the mortuary walks by is its rhythm. I came back up and told Rell and she sat down on the stair.

The intakes are where the machine takes. Six of them can be reached from the gallery walkway and one of those six has a gate that a person can move. If I close it I will find out whether the wells above are fed by this thing or merely near it, and the well above the sixth intake is the one on the Soulrest stair.

Rell says the Court cannot authorise it and cannot stop me and would like the result. Bel Mourne says that if I am right about what the intake does then somebody will die of it, and that she would still do it, and that I should be clear with myself about which of those two sentences I am acting on.
The gate is closed. The machine's rhythm did not change. Nothing down here noticed at all. I closed it myself and then I sat on the walkway and waited.

The Soulrest well went cold within the day. Sap in the basin, right colour, does nothing, exactly as at the Bone Ladder. So it is not that the machine is stealing what the wells should get. It is that the wells are drinking what the machine lets past. The sapwells work because of the thing that is killing the marsh, and I have just proved it by turning it off. One gate, one test, and whichever way I run it is the way it was run. A proof taken on paper cannot then be taken with a hand, and a well that has gone cold does not un-go cold because I changed my mind about the method.

A mortuary hand called Sesh-Weth died on the second day with the gate shut, in the ordinary way, of a chest thing he had had for years. The well did not take him. He is the only person in four hundred years of that book who went into the Soulrest ground and gave nothing back, and it is written next to my name because Ojal-Weeth writes down who was there.

I opened the gate again on the second day and the Soulrest well came back within the hour. I know what the machine does now and it cost one man who was going to die anyway and who deserved better than to be an experiment. I have written his name down here because there is nowhere else it will be written.

Hosk-Vei says the Recension does not mean that the count will be read by somebody who is owed nothing. It means the count will be read by somebody who is put into it. There is a basin on the gallery and to read what is held below I have to let the thing below hold me.

He was clear about the cost and I want it written down that he was clear. Whatever is in that basin will take my pattern and keep it, and there is no rootkeeper, no sexton, no cure and no ending that takes it back out. He said it three times and then he asked me not to decide today.
Bel Mourne says do not. Rell says it is what I am for. Ashul-Tei's question, the one she made me repeat, was for the writer of that letter, and I cannot ask it of him without going in.

I have put my hand in the basin at the seventh bay. It is cold and it is not sap. Something read me, all the way through, in about the time it takes to lose your footing, and the count of forty went out of rhythm for one cycle and came back. I am in the Count now. I do not feel changed and I am told that is normal and that it is not the same as being unchanged. There is no second reading and no other basin. What was done at the seventh bay closes every other way of doing it, and there is nothing anywhere in this province that undoes it.

What being in it gets me is that the machine now answers when I put my hand on it. Not in words. It gives me the shape of what it is holding, the way a ledger gives you a total, and the total is four thousand years of everything that has died in this province and did not get down to a root.

The other thing being in it gets me is that I cannot be re-issued clean any more. The wells still take me and what comes back is a little further from what went in each time. Hosk-Vei knew that would happen. He told me the cost and he did not tell me that part, and when I asked him why not he said that nobody who was told that part has ever gone in.

I am in the Count. It cost what I was told it would cost and one thing I was not told, and it is the only reason anything after this is possible. I have written the date down. Nobody else is going to.

Neeja-Xul says there is another way at the machine and it does not involve the Court at all. Every intake it has runs on live root. Cut the root above the intake with a proper skei and the intake stops, and eleven of them can be reached from below without ever going onto the Court's gallery. She told me how and then told me she would not come with me.

She is not offering this as a kindness. The Cutters have been blamed for thirty years for a thing they did not start and she would like the province to watch somebody cut a root for a reason it cannot argue with. She was honest about that, which I did not expect and which does not make it a better idea.

The knife is under the reed-walk in the flooded chamber. It is her grandmother's and it is the reason her grandmother's yard book exists, and she will not go in for it herself because she is afraid of what the yard would think of her for wanting it. She will not go in for it and she asked me whether I would.

I have the skei. What it opens is a route to the machine that goes under the Court, past the sextons, past the Recension and past whatever I am supposed to be, and cuts eleven live roots to get there. Everyone I have asked agrees this would stop the intakes. Nobody I have asked will say what stopping them does to the wells above, and I have already proved what stopping one does. The knife is hers or it is mine. If I keep it the route under the Court opens and the yard is owed something it will collect; if I hand it back the route closes, and it is the only door in this whole business that opens again if I ask.
The skei is in my pack. I have not decided anything by taking it, except that the decision is now mine to make, which is what she wanted and which she got.

Sesh-Anaat has sent for me by a route I do not understand — a carter at Nine-Mud knew my name and knew where I had been, and had been told at a well two days from here. The rootkeeper at Thorn says the tree has asked for me. She says trees do not do this.

The causeway out to the tree takes most of a morning and there is nothing on it. Sesh-Anaat walked it with me and did not say anything for the whole of it, and at the end she said that in forty years the tree at Thorn has spoken plainly twice, and that both times it was because it had run out of other things to do.

The tree spoke to me and it was not a dream and there was no ceremony. It said four sentences. It said that what is below Soulrest is not its enemy and never was. It said the arrangement is older than any tree standing in this province. It said that the roots have been drinking an allowance for four thousand years and have forgotten how to drink anything else. And it said: do not ask me what to do.

I asked it anyway, three times, in three different ways. It did not answer and it did not go away, and Sesh-Anaat stood in the water and cried, quietly, because a tree that will not answer a question it invited you out here to ask is a tree that does not know.

Sesh-Anaat says I must not repeat the fourth sentence to any rootkeeper in the province. The first three are theology and can be argued with. The fourth is the tree admitting it has no instruction, and she says that if that gets out, the interior will do something and it will not be a considered something. The fourth sentence is kept or it is carried, and once it has been said out loud to anyone it can never again be a thing only three of us heard.

Four sentences from a tree, and the fourth of them was that it does not know. Everyone from here on will tell me what the Hist wants. I have heard what the Hist wants and it is for somebody else to decide.

There is a way at this that does not need the Court, the chapter, the writ, the barges or the eight voices. Eleven live roots in standing water between Sunken Barrow and the Wastes, a cutter's knife, and about nine days. Neeja-Xul will not come and has told me how.

The first root took four hours and it is the smallest of the eleven. What comes out of a live root when it is opened without leave is not sap, at first. I am not going to describe it here. The intake below it stopped within the day and I felt the change through the water.

The well at Sunken Barrow went cold on the third day and the well at Mudwater Landing on the fifth. I knew this would happen. I proved it would happen with my own hand on the sixth intake and a man is buried for it. I am doing it anyway and I want that written down in the order it happened.

Six of eleven and the interior has worked out what is doing it. There are keepers standing at the seventh root. They are not armed and they are not going to move and there is no way to open that root that does not go through where they are standing. I am the thing they are standing there about.

Eleven roots in nineteen days. The keepers at the seventh moved, in the end, because Neeja-Xul came out and stood between us and talked to them for a night, and she has not spoken to me since. The intakes are shut and the way down through the root channels is open and there are nine wells cold between here and Soulrest.

The channels go in under the Wastes below the crypt road, below the gallery, below the ash. They are empty now because I emptied them. It is four days in the dark with the walls going soft where the roots were and there is no camp, no writ, no barges and nobody behind me.

I came up into the working parts from underneath, which nobody has done, and the keepers on the counting floor did not know I was there for a day and a half. Two of the bays are dead already, from the roots I cut, and the people who kept them are sitting in them.

Ixtu-Meer knew. He has known since the third root. He has been sitting in the counting chamber for nineteen days with a ledger going wrong in front of him and no way to stop it and no interest in leaving, and when I came up out of the floor he asked whether I had come the long way and whether I wanted to sit down.

The conversation is the same conversation. He makes the same case, which is still good, and this time I have already done half of what he is arguing against and he knows it and he makes it anyway. The reservoir is bleeding through six shut intakes into channels I opened and it will empty on its own in about a season whatever either of us does.

I opened the last sluices from below and the Count went down into the channels I had cut for it rather than into the roots, which is not what opening it was supposed to mean. Four thousand years of pattern went past the trees entirely and into the dark. The wells will not come back. Ixtu-Meer watched the whole of it from the stair and said one thing at the end, which was that this was also a way.
